final_answer:
In an economic system where prices are determined by the interaction of buyers and sellers, the price of a good or service is established at the point where the quantity demanded by consumers equals the quantity supplied by producers. When demand for a product increases (e.g., due to higher consumer interest or scarcity), buyers are willing to pay more, which drives prices upward. Conversely, if supply increases (e.g., due to greater production capacity or lower production costs), sellers may lower prices to attract buyers. This dynamic equilibrium between willingness to pay and willingness to sell sets the price.

When a government intervenes by setting a maximum price (a price ceiling) below this equilibrium, it can create imbalances. At the lower price, producers may find it unprofitable to supply the same quantity as before, leading to reduced production or withdrawal from the system. Simultaneously, consumers may demand more of the product because it is cheaper. This mismatch between supply and demand results in shortages. Over time, this can lead to black markets, reduced quality of goods or services, or allocation through non-price mechanisms like queues or rationing. The policy may also discourage innovation or investment in the affected sector.
